comment.comment: Spec §Comment (fork v1.2): whole lines between `<!--` at the start of a line and `-->` followed only by blanks. Must be tried before #title, which would otherwise claim the opening line. An unterminated comment runs to the end of the file, as the spec requires.
comment.name: comment.block.xit markup.other.comment.xit

title.comment: A marked title, and a fork of the specification. Spec §Title defines a title by what it is not - "MUST NOT start with a blank character or `[`" - which leaves the format with no invalid state for a line: anything that fails to be an item is silently promoted to a heading, so `- [ ] Buy milk` becomes one and the task disappears. A marker turns that into an error you can see. `#` then a space, or `#` alone: the space is what keeps it clear of a tag, since a tag needs a name character straight after the hash. See src/title.ts.
title.name: markup.underline.xit markup.other.task.title.xit

invalid.comment: A line that is not a comment, not an item, and not a title. This rule only exists because titles are marked; without a marker every one of these would be a heading. It must come last in the top-level patterns, so it only sees what the others declined. Continuation lines never reach it - they are matched inside the item rule - and neither do blank lines, which match nothing at all.
invalid.name: invalid.illegal.xit markup.other.task.invalid.xit

open-item.comment: Spec §Item: an item starts at the beginning of a line. The empty capture group is there only so the end pattern can be written once and shared with the nested form, where it back-references the parent's indentation.

closed-item.comment: Spec §Item: an item starts at the beginning of a line. The empty capture group is there only so the end pattern can be written once and shared with the nested form, where it back-references the parent's indentation.

subitem.comment: Nested items. Included from inside an item only, never at the top level.

open-subitem.comment: A subtask: an item indented from its parent by one tab per level. Spaces do not nest, and that is a fork of our own earlier fork: 'two or more spaces, or one tab' let a single stray space create a level, silently, and made a three-space line a child of a two-space one. A tab is a level, a space at the start of an item is a mistake, and diagnostics say so. This rule is reachable only from inside another item, which is what stops an indented checkbox with nothing above it from counting - the specification says a checkbox cannot be preceded by whitespace, and outside a parent that still holds. The end pattern back-references the parent's indentation, which is the only way a nested rule can find its parent's edge: TextMate cannot count indentation, but it can compare a line against the exact prefix that was matched. Nesting is a fork of the specification, which has none - see discussion #2. A tab also continues a description, which the specification does not allow - it asks for exactly four spaces, and the syntax guide lists a tab as invalid. Forked so that the Tab key works everywhere in the file rather than nesting subtasks but breaking continuations.

closed-subitem.comment: A subtask: an item indented from its parent by one tab per level. Spaces do not nest, and that is a fork of our own earlier fork: 'two or more spaces, or one tab' let a single stray space create a level, silently, and made a three-space line a child of a two-space one. A tab is a level, a space at the start of an item is a mistake, and diagnostics say so. This rule is reachable only from inside another item, which is what stops an indented checkbox with nothing above it from counting - the specification says a checkbox cannot be preceded by whitespace, and outside a parent that still holds. The end pattern back-references the parent's indentation, which is the only way a nested rule can find its parent's edge: TextMate cannot count indentation, but it can compare a line against the exact prefix that was matched. Nesting is a fork of the specification, which has none - see discussion #2.

closed-body.comment: The struck-through part of a closed item: its description, and not its subtasks. This used to be a contentName on closed-item itself, which painted the whole begin/end region - and a subtask lives inside that region, so an open subtask under a checked parent rendered as though it were done. TextMate scopes are additive, so the subtask could not undo it. Ending at any line that starts with a checkbox hands those lines back to closed-item, which matches them with #subitem instead. After the subtask closes, this rule starts again for whatever description follows. Its end has to cover the end of the item as well as a subtask, because TextMate only tests the end of the innermost rule on the stack - relying on the enclosing item to pop this one let it run past a blank line and swallow the next title as struck-through description. So it ends at a line holding a checkbox, at a blank line, and at any line starting in column zero.

priority.comment: Priority is exclamation marks, and this fork has dropped the dots. Spec §Priority allows "any number of exclamation marks (`!`) and dots (`.`)" with the dots on one side only, and the guide's priority/1 says why they exist: "The priority can be padded with dots on either side" - they are alignment filler, so the exclamation marks line up in a column. That is visual presentation stored in the file, and three of the guide's seven priority rules exist only to police it. An editor can draw the column with a decoration and put nothing in the document, which is what decorations are for. Spec §Item allows additional space characters between the checkbox and the priority, so the separator is `[^\S\n]+` rather than a single space.

due-date.comment: Spec §Due Date: `-> ` followed by yyyy, yyyy-mm, yyyy-mm-dd, yyyy-Www or yyyy-Qq, with `-` or `/` as separator. The two lookbehinds are the left-hand boundary the syntax guide describes as "Due dates can be surrounded by a space or punctuation (apart from a hyphen or slash)": the first rejects a letter or digit before the arrow, so `Due-> 2022-01-31` is not a date, and the second rejects a hyphen or slash, so `---> 2022-01-31` is not one either. Both are negative, so a date at the very start of a description still matches. The backreference to group 5 forces one separator style per date. Trailing junk is rejected, but calendar validity beyond simple ranges cannot be checked here. This is a begin/end rule rather than a plain match so that the remainder of the item is tokenized without the due-date pattern: that is how "any additional due dates MUST be disregarded" is enforced. Its end is the end of the enclosing item, so the rule holds across continuation lines too. It also ends at any line holding a checkbox, because a subtask starts a new item and gets a due date of its own.

tag.comment: Spec §Tag: the name is letters (Unicode L), digits, `_` or `-`. The `(?<=[\s\p{P}])` lookbehind is a deliberate divergence, and Discussion #51 is the thing to read before removing it: asked whether `a#tag` holds a tag, jotaen answered "Currently, yes", and named the consequences as accepted downsides (`bN144#y6Q!Jc` yields the tag `#y6Q`). The spec is silent on what may precede a `#`, so it agrees with him. His own xit-sublime rule carries this lookbehind regardless, so the reference implementation contradicts the answer, and it is the better behaviour. An unquoted value uses the same set; a quoted value may hold anything but its own quote, and an unterminated quote means the value is absent. The `=` is captured on its own, and the value after it is optional, because the spec says an empty tag value "MUST be treated the same as an absent tag value". So `#tag=` colours as one tag rather than leaving the `=` uncoloured in the middle of one, and `#tag="unterminated` colours as `#tag=` with the rest falling back to description. The `=` carries the tag scope but not the value scope: there is no value there to name.
